fields.independence_analysis: The three assertions come from three distinct original records. The 1850 census (a_002, src_001) and the 1860 census (a_009, src_003) are different government records taken by different enumerators ten years apart, so as source records they are independent of each other. For Patrick's birthplace specifically, however, both censuses most likely drew on the same underlying household knowledge — a member of the Thomas Flynn household (probably Thomas or his wife) reporting the same fact at both enumerations. This makes them partially dependent for the Ireland claim: they are not two fully independent evidentiary paths but rather the same family's report recorded twice a decade apart. That said, consistent reporting across two separate enumerations — with different enumerators, different years, and no evident copying — carries meaningfully more weight than a single record. The 1908 death certificate (a_012, src_004) is fully independent of both censuses: a different record type created nearly six decades later, with a different and identified informant (James Brown, son-in-law). In sum: two partially dependent assertions supporting Ireland, one fully independent assertion supporting Pennsylvania, but the fully independent assertion comes from a substantially weaker informant for this particular fact.
fields.weighing_analysis: Two factors are decisive. First, informant proximity and temporal distance from the birth event: the census informants were almost certainly household members — most likely Patrick's own parents — reporting a birthplace that was only 5 to 15 years in the past. James Brown, by contrast, was a son-in-law filing a death certificate in 1908, reporting on a birth he could not have witnessed and that occurred roughly 63 years before he put pen to paper. He is classified as family_not_present and secondary for birth information, while the census informants, though technically 'unknown,' were almost certainly persons with direct family knowledge. Second, consistency: two census records taken a decade apart record Ireland without variation. Even granting partial dependence on the same household informant, a consistent answer across two independent enumerations is substantially stronger than one contrary claim. The death certificate is authoritative for facts James Brown could know firsthand — the date and place of Patrick's death — but that strength does not extend to a birth he never witnessed. Defensible rationale: the Pennsylvania claim is both uncorroborated (one record, one informant) and substantially less credible for this fact (secondary informant, 63-year gap), satisfying rationales 1 and 2 in combination.
fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is disputed between Ireland, reported in the 1850 and 1860 federal census records, and Pennsylvania, reported in his 1908 death certificate. Resolving the birthplace matters directly for the primary research question: whether the family immigrated from Ireland shapes where records of Patrick's origins and parentage would be found.

The 1850 census is an original federal record taken when Patrick was approximately 5 years old, listing his birthplace as Ireland while he resided in the Thomas Flynn household in Schuylkill County. The 1860 census, another original federal record taken ten years later, records the same household with Patrick now approximately 15 years old, again giving Ireland as his birthplace. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate, completed by James Brown — Patrick's son-in-law — gives Pennsylvania as his birthplace.

The two census records are far more reliable for Patrick's birthplace. Both were created within living memory of his birth, and the likely informant — a household member such as Thomas Flynn or his wife — would have had direct, firsthand knowledge of where their son was born. James Brown had no such knowledge. He was a son-in-law filing paperwork while grieving, reporting on a birth that occurred decades before he was part of the family. The combination of two consistent contemporary records from well-positioned informants against one late secondary report is decisive: Ireland is preferred.

The death certificate's 'Pennsylvania' most likely reflects the well-documented immigration-origin confusion pattern. Patrick spent the bulk of his life as a Pennsylvania resident; Brown knew the family only as Pennsylvanians. Asked for a birthplace he could not know firsthand, he reported the family's long-familiar home state rather than the foreign country of actual birth. This conflation of enduring residence with origin is especially common when an immigrant's American relatives have no living memory of the old-country connection.

The conflict between the census records and the death certificate comes down to informant quality and proximity to the fact:

As source documents they are independent. As information units, however, they are partially dependent: the underlying knowledge in both almost certainly flowed from the same household member — Thomas Flynn or his wife — responding to the enumerator's questions about Patrick's birthplace on two different occasions. fields.weighing_analysis: The decisive factors are informant proximity and temporal distance from the event. The census records were completed by a household member — most plausibly Thomas Flynn or his wife — who could speak from direct knowledge about where Patrick was born. The 1850 census was compiled when Patrick was approximately five years old, within living memory of the birth; the 1860 record repeats the same claim a decade later. James Brown, the death certificate informant, is identified as the son-in-law: he had no firsthand knowledge of a birth that preceded any family connection with him, and he reported in 1908 — roughly 63 years after the event. The death certificate is an original record for the facts of death (date, cause, place of death) but carries only secondary information about birth facts, because the informant was not present at and cannot have known the birth from experience. Two partially dependent but temporally proximate census entries, each from a household informant with direct knowledge, substantially outweigh one late statement from a secondary informant. fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County census records both record Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. Establishing the correct birthplace matters directly to the primary research question — if Patrick was born in Ireland, his parents were immigrants and parent-search strategies must focus on Irish emigration and pre-emigration records; if he was born in Pennsylvania, entirely different record sets apply.

The 1850 U.S. Census (Schuylkill County, dwelling 84) lists Patrick, then about five years old, with Ireland as birthplace. The 1860 U.S. Census (dwelling 112) lists him again at approximately fifteen, again with Ireland. In both cases a household member — almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — provided the birthplace information to the visiting enumerator. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate records Pennsylvania as the birthplace; the identified informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law.

Ireland is the more reliable answer. The census records were made while Patrick was a child living with the family members best positioned to know his origins. The 1850 record comes just five years after the birth. James Brown, by contrast, was Patrick's son-in-law: he entered the family as an adult, could have had no firsthand knowledge of a birth 63 years before the death certificate was filed, and was reporting secondhand from what he had heard or assumed. Two census records with household-informant testimony, each recorded close to the event and during Patrick's childhood, substantially outweigh a single late statement by a secondary informant.

The error on the death certificate follows the well-documented immigration-origin confusion pattern. Patrick Flynn was born in Ireland but had lived in Pennsylvania for decades by 1908 — almost certainly arriving as a small child around 1845–1850. James Brown knew Patrick exclusively as a Pennsylvania man: his home, work, children, and entire adult life were rooted there. A son-in-law reporting a birth he could not have witnessed, 63 years after the fact, would naturally supply the family's long-established Pennsylvania address as the birthplace — the locally familiar answer in place of a geographic origin he had no personal knowledge of and no reason to investigate. The result is a plausible but incorrect Pennsylvania birthplace on the death certificate, entered against two census records made when the Irish birth was still a living family memory.

c_001 is resolved. Two other conflicts remain open (c_002 and c_003 — both identity questions about whether the Patrick Flynn in specific census records is the same person as the research subject); those are set aside for separate invocations since c_001 is the most foundational fact conflict and the one you asked about.

**c_001 — resolved, preferred assertion a_002 (Ireland)**

The 1850 and 1860 census records both give Ireland; the 1908 death certificate gives Pennsylvania. The death certificate informant was James Brown, the son-in-law, reporting 63 years after the birth — a fact he could not have witnessed and had no firsthand way to know. The census records were completed by a household member (most likely Thomas Flynn or his wife) within a decade of the birth event, when the Irish origin was living family knowledge. The census pair, though partially dependent on the same informant's knowledge, substantially outweighs the single late secondary-informant entry on the death certificate.

---

Two records disagreed about where Patrick Flynn was born. The 1850 and 1860 census records, filled out when Patrick was a child living with his family, both say Ireland. The 1908 death certificate says Pennsylvania. The person who reported Patrick's birthplace on the death certificate was his son-in-law, James Brown — someone who married into the family as an adult and had no way to personally know where his father-in-law was born over sixty years earlier. He almost certainly knew Patrick only as a lifelong Pennsylvania man, and gave Pennsylvania as the answer because that was all he knew. The two census entries, made while Patrick was young and while the family's Irish origin was still recent memory, are far more reliable for this fact.

With Patrick's Irish birth confirmed, the search for his parents should now focus on Irish emigration records and pre-emigration sources, not Pennsylvania birth records.

weighing_analysis.after: The decisive factors are informant proximity and temporal distance from the event. The census records were completed by a household member — most plausibly Thomas Flynn or his wife — who could speak from direct knowledge about where Patrick was born. The 1850 census was compiled when Patrick was approximately five years old, within living memory of the birth; the 1860 record repeats the same claim a decade later. James Brown, the death certificate informant, is identified as the son-in-law: he had no firsthand knowledge of a birth that preceded any family connection with him, and he reported in 1908 — roughly 63 years after the event. The death certificate is an original record for the facts of death but carries only secondary information about birth facts, because the informant was not present at and cannot have known the birth from experience. Two partially dependent but temporally proximate census entries, each from a household informant with direct knowledge, substantially outweigh one late statement from a secondary informant. The applicable defensible rationales are: (1) more error-prone source — for the specific fact of birthplace, the death certificate is a secondary-informant entry filed decades after the event; (2) uncorroborated single item — the Pennsylvania claim stands alone against two census records.

resolution_rationale.after:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County census records both record Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. Establishing the correct birthplace matters directly to the primary research question — if Patrick was born in Ireland, his parents were immigrants and parent-search strategies must focus on Irish emigration and pre-emigration records; if he was born in Pennsylvania, entirely different record sets apply.

The 1850 U.S. Census (Schuylkill County, dwelling 84) lists Patrick, then about five years old, with Ireland as birthplace. The 1860 U.S. Census (dwelling 112) lists him again at approximately fifteen, again with Ireland. In both cases a household member — almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — provided the birthplace information to the visiting enumerator. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate records Pennsylvania as the birthplace; the identified informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law.

Ireland is the more reliable answer. The census records were made while Patrick was a child living with the family members best positioned to know his origins. The 1850 record comes just five years after the birth. James Brown, by contrast, was Patrick's son-in-law: he entered the family as an adult, could have had no firsthand knowledge of a birth 63 years before the death certificate was filed, and was reporting secondhand from what he had heard or assumed. Two census records with household-informant testimony, each recorded close to the event and during Patrick's childhood, substantially outweigh a single late statement by a secondary informant.

The error on the death certificate follows the well-documented immigration-origin confusion pattern. Patrick Flynn was born in Ireland but had lived in Pennsylvania for decades by 1908 — almost certainly arriving as a small child around 1845–1850. James Brown knew Patrick exclusively as a Pennsylvania man: his home, work, children, and entire adult life were rooted there. A son-in-law reporting a birth he could not have witnessed, 63 years after the fact, would naturally supply the family's long-established Pennsylvania address as the birthplace — the locally familiar answer in place of a geographic origin he had no personal knowledge of and no reason to investigate. The result is a plausible but incorrect Pennsylvania birthplace on the death certificate, entered against two census records made when the Irish birth was still a living family memory.

independence_analysis.after: a_002 (1850 census) and a_009 (1860 census) are separate original government records created by different enumerators a decade apart. As source documents they are independent. As information units, however, they are partially dependent: the underlying knowledge in both almost certainly flowed from the same household member — Thomas Flynn or his wife — responding to the enumerator's questions about Patrick's birthplace on two different occasions. The same individual's stated knowledge is the root of both readings, so the census pair constitutes a partially corroborated unit rather than two fully independent lines of evidence. a_012 (the 1908 death certificate, informant James Brown) draws on a completely different informant — the son-in-law — who had no connection to either census enumeration. It is fully independent of the census pair but stands alone on the Pennsylvania claim.

fields.independence_analysis: The three sources bearing on this identity question are fully independent. The 1850 Schuylkill County census (src_001) was created by a government enumerator who physically visited the household in 1850. The 1860 Schuylkill County census (src_003) was recorded by a separate government enumerator ten years later, under a different microfilm roll and dwelling number, for a separate federal enumeration. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (src_004) was completed by a different government official in 1908, relying on information supplied by son-in-law James Brown — a distinct recorder, a distinct informant, and a different administrative purpose. None of these three sources derives from any of the others. The Ancestry index (src_002) is a transcription of src_001 and is not independent of it; it plays no role in this identity question.
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors are decisive. First, age consistency across two independent enumerations: Patrick Flynn appears in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household in 1850 (age 5, dwelling 84) and again in 1860 (age 15, dwelling 112). The age difference of exactly ten years across a ten-year interval is internally consistent and confirms a single individual. Two enumerators, a decade apart, independently recording the same person in the same family is the strongest positive-identification pattern census research affords. Second, the 1908 death certificate directly names Thomas Flynn as father — aligning with the household head in both censuses. The informant (son-in-law James Brown) had secondary knowledge of the birth facts, but naming the father's given name and surname is a direct family-knowledge claim unlikely to be fabricated for a common Irish name. Third, the competing candidate (household 197, Patrick Flynn age 6 in 1850) leaves no subsequent record connecting him to Thomas Flynn. The 1860 census search examined five results and returned only one Thomas Flynn household with a Patrick Flynn son — meaning no competing Thomas Flynn family carried a Patrick Flynn forward to 1860. Positive placement across three independent sources over 58 years constitutes clear preponderance.
fields.resolution_rationale:
The problem: Two boys named Patrick Flynn of similar ages appear in Schuylkill County's 1850 census — one aged 5 in dwelling 84 under Thomas Flynn, and one aged 6 in dwelling 197 under an unidentified head. The 1908 death certificate for a Patrick Flynn who died in Schuylkill County names Thomas Flynn as father but gives no earlier household reference, leaving open which 1850 Patrick is the 1908 decedent.

The conflicting evidence: The 1850 census (src_001) places Patrick Flynn, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household 84. fields.independence_analysis: Three source groups bear on this identity question, and all three are independent in origin and purpose. The 1850 census (src_001) is an original record created by a census enumerator visiting the Thomas Flynn household in dwelling 84. The 1860 census (src_003) is a separate original record created by a different enumerator ten years later, visiting dwelling 112. Although the two census records may share the same household's knowledge base for facts such as age and birthplace, they independently attest that the same child was present in the Thomas Flynn household at both enumeration dates — the enumerators and the occasions of recording were distinct. The 1908 death certificate (src_004) is fully independent of both census records: it was created 48 to 58 years later by a different authority (the Pennsylvania Department of Health) for a different purpose (registering a death), with James Brown (son-in-law) as the informant for biographical facts. James Brown's knowledge of his father-in-law's parentage — specifically his naming of Thomas Flynn as father — derived from family history transmitted through his wife, not from any census record. The death certificate's naming of Thomas Flynn as father is therefore an independent evidentiary thread, not a re-statement of census information.
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors are decisive. First, birth-year consistency: the death certificate states a birth year of 1845, which matches the household 84 child (age 5 in 1850, implying birth ~1845), and does not match the competing household 197 child (age 6 in 1850, implying birth ~1844). A one-year difference is small but directionally consistent with household 84 and inconsistent with household 197. Second, parental identification: the 1908 death certificate independently names Thomas Flynn as father. This is a specific claim — not merely a common name but the specific father's name — that directly connects the decedent to the Thomas Flynn household. For this coincidence to favor household 197, there would have to be a second Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County in 1850 with a son named Patrick born the same year, which is not in evidence. Third, ten-year continuity: the 1860 census independently shows a Patrick Flynn, age 15, still enumerated in Thomas Flynn's household. Age 15 in 1860 implies birth ~1845, consistent only with the household 84 child, not the household 197 child (who would be 16 in 1860). All three independent sources converge on the same individual. The second candidate (household 197) is not corroborated by any record after 1850 and cannot be positively advanced as an alternative.
fields.resolution_rationale:
Two Patrick Flynns of similar age appeared in Schuylkill County in 1850, raising the question of which one corresponds to the Patrick Flynn on the 1908 death certificate. Answering this is foundational: until the identity is confirmed, no parentage conclusion can rest on the Thomas Flynn household records.

The Thomas Flynn household (dwelling 84) contained a Patrick Flynn, age 5 in 1850, giving a birth year of approximately 1845. The same household appears in the 1860 census (dwelling 112) with a Patrick Flynn now age 15, consistent with birth ~1845. The competing candidate appeared in dwelling 197 in 1850 at age 6, implying birth approximately 1844. The 1908 death certificate, supplied by son-in-law James Brown, gives Patrick's birth year as 1845 and names Thomas Flynn as the deceased's father.

The convergence of three independent sources resolves the question. The death certificate birth year (1845) matches the household 84 child, not the household 197 child (born ~1844). More decisively, the death certificate independently names Thomas Flynn as father — the same Thomas Flynn who headed the 1850 and 1860 households. This naming was not derived from the census records; it was reported by a son-in-law from his knowledge of his wife's family history. The 1860 census further confirms continuity: Patrick is still in the Thomas Flynn household at age 15, consistent only with the household 84 child. For the household 197 candidate to be the decedent, a second unrecorded Thomas Flynn in the same county would have to have fathered a son named Patrick in the same year — a coincidence with no evidentiary support.

James Brown's report is secondary information (he was not present at his father-in-law's birth), which is a normal limitation of death certificate parentage data. The specific naming of Thomas Flynn, corroborated by two census records placing Patrick in exactly that household, satisfies the preponderance standard. The assertion linking the Thomas Flynn 1850 household child to the research subject (a_001) is the preferred finding. The identity is confirmed: the Patrick Flynn in dwelling 84 of the 1850 Thomas Flynn household is the Patrick Flynn who died in 1908.

Here is the conflict-resolution agent's full report:

---

**Important distinction up front:** "Original vs. derivative" describes the *source format* (how the record came to us). "Primary vs. secondary" describes the *information quality* (whether the informant had firsthand knowledge of the event). These two axes are independent — an original source can contain secondary information, and a derivative can transmit primary information. That combination appears clearly in the death certificate below.

---

## Source 1 — 1850 U.S. Census, FamilySearch image (src_001)

**Format: Original.** This is the NARA microfilm image of the census itself, accessed through FamilySearch.

| Assertion | Fact | Information quality | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_001 | Patrick Flynn — name | Indeterminate | The informant who supplied the name to the enumerator is unknown; could be a household member or a neighbor |
| a_002 | Birth ~1845, Ireland (age 5) | Indeterminate | Age and birthplace had to be reported by someone, almost certainly a household member, but the census does not identify who |
| a_003 | Residence, Schuylkill County, PA | **Primary** | The enumerator is a firsthand witness to residence — they visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This is the one fact the enumerator knew directly |
| a_004 | Relationship: listed in Thomas Flynn household, position consistent with child | Indeterminate | No relationship column existed in 1850; this is a researcher inference from household position and surname, not a reported fact |
| a_005 | Thomas Flynn — name (head of household) | Indeterminate | Likely Thomas supplied his own name, but the census does not identify the informant |

---

## Source 2 — 1850 U.S. Census, Ancestry index (src_002)

**Format: Derivative.** This is Ancestry's transcribed index of the identical underlying census. It is not an independent source — it is a copy of src_001 and the two count as a single evidentiary unit.

| Assertion | Fact | Information quality | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_006 | Patrick Flynn — name | Indeterminate | Transcribed from the same record as a_001; no independent informant |
| a_007 | Birth ~1845, Ireland (age 5) | Indeterminate | Same as above; transcription of a_002 |

These two assertions add no independent weight beyond src_001 — a_006 corroborates a_001 and a_007 corroborates a_002 only in the sense of confirming the transcription is consistent, not as an independent source of the same fact.

---

## Source 3 — 1860 U.S. Census, FamilySearch image (src_003)

**Format: Original.** NARA microfilm of the 1860 population schedule, accessed through FamilySearch.

| Assertion | Fact | Information quality | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_008 | Patrick Flynn — name | Indeterminate | Same reasoning as a_001; informant unknown |

| a_010 | Relationship: household position consistent with son of Thomas Flynn | Indeterminate | 1860 also lacked a relationship column; researcher inference from position, age, and shared surname |

Note: a_009's birthplace "Ireland" conflicts directly with a_012's "Pennsylvania" from the death certificate. This is already tracked as unresolved conflict **c_001**, which is blocking question q_001 (Patrick's parentage).

## Source 4 — 1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate (src_004)

**Format: Original.** The government vital record itself, accessed through FamilySearch from the Pennsylvania State Archives.

This source illustrates why the two axes matter: the *document* is original, but the *information* it carries is split between primary and secondary depending on which fact and which informant contributed it.

| a_013 | Father: Thomas Flynn | **Secondary** | Same informant; reporting family history passed down to him, not something he observed firsthand |

I now have everything needed. Here is the full classification of all thirteen assertions across four sources.

---

**Important distinction up front:** "Original vs. derivative" describes the *source format* (how the record came to us). "Primary vs. secondary" describes the *information quality* (whether the informant had firsthand knowledge of the event). These two axes are independent — an original source can contain secondary information, and a derivative can transmit primary information. That combination appears clearly in the death certificate below.

---

## Source 1 — 1850 U.S. Census, FamilySearch image (src_001)

**Format: Original.** This is the NARA microfilm image of the census itself, accessed through FamilySearch.

| Assertion | Fact | Information quality | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_001 | Patrick Flynn — name | Indeterminate | The informant who supplied the name to the enumerator is unknown; could be a household member or a neighbor |
| a_002 | Birth ~1845, Ireland (age 5) | Indeterminate | Age and birthplace had to be reported by someone, almost certainly a household member, but the census does not identify who |
| a_003 | Residence, Schuylkill County, PA | **Primary** | The enumerator is a firsthand witness to residence — they visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This is the one fact the enumerator knew directly |
| a_004 | Relationship: listed in Thomas Flynn household, position consistent with child | Indeterminate | No relationship column existed in 1850; this is a researcher inference from household position and surname, not a reported fact |
| a_005 | Thomas Flynn — name (head of household) | Indeterminate | Likely Thomas supplied his own name, but the census does not identify the informant |

---

## Source 2 — 1850 U.S. Census, Ancestry index (src_002)

**Format: Derivative.** This is Ancestry's transcribed index of the identical underlying census. It is not an independent source — it is a copy of src_001 and the two count as a single evidentiary unit.

| Assertion | Fact | Information quality | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_006 | Patrick Flynn — name | Indeterminate | Transcribed from the same record as a_001; no independent informant |
| a_007 | Birth ~1845, Ireland (age 5) | Indeterminate | Same as above; transcription of a_002 |

These two assertions add no independent weight beyond src_001 — a_006 corroborates a_001 and a_007 corroborates a_002 only in the sense of confirming the transcription is consistent, not as an independent source of the same fact.

---

## Source 3 — 1860 U.S. Census, FamilySearch image (src_003)

**Format: Original.** NARA microfilm of the 1860 population schedule, accessed through FamilySearch.

| Assertion | Fact | Information quality | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_008 | Patrick Flynn — name | Indeterminate | Same reasoning as a_001; informant unknown |
| a_009 | Birth ~1845, Ireland (age 15) | Indeterminate | Age and birthplace reported by unknown household informant to enumerator; residence column for birthplace is indeterminate |
| a_010 | Relationship: household position consistent with son of Thomas Flynn | Indeterminate | 1860 also lacked a relationship column; researcher inference from position, age, and shared surname |

Note: a_009's birthplace "Ireland" conflicts directly with a_012's "Pennsylvania" from the death certificate. This is already tracked as unresolved conflict c_001, which currently blocks question q_001 (Patrick's parentage).

---

## Source 4 — 1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate (src_004)

**Format: Original.** The government vital record itself, accessed through FamilySearch from the Pennsylvania State Archives.

This source illustrates why the two axes matter: the *document* is original, but the *information* it carries is split between primary and secondary depending on which fact and which informant contributed it.

| Assertion | Fact | Information quality | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_012 | Birth 1845, Pennsylvania | **Secondary** | Informant James Brown (son-in-law) reported birth facts he did not witness, decades after the event. He was not present at Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told — or what he assumed |
| a_013 | Father: Thomas Flynn | **Secondary** | Same informant, same reasoning. Brown is reporting family history passed down to him, not something he observed firsthand |

The death certificate *does* carry primary information for the death itself (date, place, cause), but no assertions for those facts appear to have been extracted yet — the two extracted assertions concern birth and parentage, both of which fall to the secondary informant.

---

| Assertion | Source | Source format | Information quality |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_001 | 1850 census (FamilySearch) | Original | Indeterminate |
| a_002 | 1850 census (FamilySearch) | Original | Indeterminate |

| a_012 | Death certificate 1908 | Original | **Secondary** |
| a_013 | Death certificate 1908 | Original | **Secondary** |

Everything else is indeterminate (unknown informant in the censuses) or secondary (son-in-law on the death certificate). This is normal for 19th-century records but does mean the evidence base is weaker than it might appear.

output.text_response:
**c_002 — unresolved (identity)**

Two tree persons named Thomas Flynn (I2 and I3) were proposed as Patrick Flynn's (I1) biological father, triggering the refused tree write. The conflict has been recorded and analyzed:

---

**Finding:** I3 Thomas Flynn is definitively excluded as Patrick's father. His date of death is recorded as **15 September 1840** — nearly five years before the **3 August 1845 baptism** that names the father as Thomas Flynn. It is a chronological impossibility for I3 to be the man named in that record.

Because this is a "different persons" conclusion (I3 is simply *not* the father in the baptism), no preferred assertion can be named for the conflict, and it remains `unresolved` in the schema per the rules for identity conflicts. However, the exclusion **unblocks the tree write** for the relationship to I2.

---

**What remains open:**

The identity of the Thomas Flynn in the baptism still needs to be confirmed as I2. The wife's name "Mary" in the baptism matches the wife in I2's 1842 Philadelphia marriage record, but no record yet places I2 in Luzerne County around 1845.

**Recommended next steps:**

1. **person-evidence** — Remove the incorrect person-evidence link `pe_010` (which ties assertion `a_018` to I3) and re-evaluate `a_018`.
2. **research-plan** — Search for a Luzerne County record placing Thomas Flynn (I2) and his wife Mary there before August 1845 to confirm the baptism father is indeed I2.

output.text_response:
**c_001 — status: unresolved**

The 1875 census "Anders Pedersen" and your subject "Anders Hansen" are almost certainly **different people**, but the conflict cannot be formally closed yet because no record directly names the census child's father.

---

**The key finding: the patronymic**

Norway ran a living patronymic system in 1875 — surnames were not fixed by law until 1923. "Pedersen" encodes *son of Peder*; "Hansen" encodes *son of Hans*. Your subject is the son of Hans Olsen and must therefore be "Hansen," not "Pedersen." This is not a spelling variant — the two roots are entirely different given names, and no transcription error bridges *Peder* and *Hans*.

The surface agreement (same given name, same age, same district) is exactly what one expects when two ordinary Norwegian families in the same parish each had a boy named Anders born around 1868 — a situation made very likely by the traditional convention of honouring the paternal grandfather.

---

**Why it stays unresolved**

Because the exclusion is not yet documented by a record that *directly* names the census child's father as Peder, `preferred_assertion_id` must remain null and status stays unresolved. This blocks q_001.

---

**What would decide it**

The decisive record is a **baptismal register entry, farm book listing, or confirmation record (~1882)** showing that the 1875 census "Anders Pedersen" was born to a father named Peder. Norwegian church books for the relevant district (e.g., Ringsaker, Hedmark) are the natural source. Once that confirms his father was Peder and not Hans, the record can be formally ruled out and the question closed.

The problem: a 1875 Norway census entry for 'Anders Pedersen,' age 7, Ringsaker, Hedmark, has been proposed as a match for the research subject Anders Hansen (born approximately 1868, son of Hans Olsen, same district). Linking it would be a key source for the subject's early life; incorrectly linking it would misattribute another child's record.

The conflicting evidence: The 1875 census records a boy named Anders Pedersen, age 7, in Ringsaker — giving name, approximate birth year (~1868), and place that surface-match the subject. The subject is independently known to be Anders Hansen, son of Hans Olsen, born approximately 1868 in the same district. The census record and the subject's identity evidence come from entirely different sources.

Why these are almost certainly different people: Norway used a living patronymic surname system in 1875; the Norwegian Names Act fixing surnames was not passed until 1923. In this system the surname directly encodes the father's given name: 'Pedersen' means son of Peder, 'Hansen' means son of Hans. Because the subject's father is Hans Olsen, the subject's patronymic must be Hansen — not Pedersen. These two surnames cannot belong to the same boy unless his father was simultaneously named Peder and Hans, which is impossible. A patronymic mismatch in a functioning patronymic system is not a spelling variant; it names a different father and therefore a different child. The shared given name, age, and district are consistent with two ordinary Norwegian families in the same parish — a plausible and common situation given traditional naming patterns that often produced multiple boys named Anders of the same generation in one district.

Why the confusion arose: Genealogical database searches retrieve records by given name, approximate birth year, and location without filtering on patronymic root. A researcher treating 'Pedersen' and 'Hansen' as surname variants — the logic appropriate to fixed surnames — would surface this record as a strong candidate. The patronymic system makes that logic inapplicable here.

What would confirm exclusion: A farm book, baptismal register, or confirmation record identifying the father of the census 'Anders Pedersen' as a man named Peder would definitively establish that this child is not the son of Hans Olsen. Until that record is found, the analysis strongly indicates these are different persons, but the conflict is recorded as unresolved because the exclusion is not yet documented by a record that directly names both the census child's father and our subject's father in the same source or corroborating pair.

The dispute concerns the first name of the mother of Cornelis van Noord, as recorded in his 1828 birth act versus a ten-year marriage index compiled between 1838 and 1848. Getting the name right matters because it governs which woman can be linked to Cornelis in subsequent records.

The birth act records the mother's name with an uncertain first letter — machine OCR gives 'Jannetje,' the researcher reads 'Tannetje' — and the surname 'van Noord' is uncontested. The index gives 'Fannetje van Noord.' These are three possible readings of what is almost certainly one name in one letter-form.

The birth act is the controlling source. Its informant was the father, present at the birth, reporting to the civil registrar on the day of the event: he was in every respect a firsthand witness to his wife's name. The index clerk, compiling summaries from marriage paperwork a decade or more later, had no such direct knowledge. On informant proximity, contemporaneity, and format, the birth act is superior in every dimension.

The preferred reading is therefore from the birth act (a_002), with the caveat that the exact first letter — J or T — remains open within that document and is captured in its recorded value as 'Jannetje [?] van Noord.'

The 'Fannetje' reading in the index is best explained as a paleographic transcription error. In early 19th-century Dutch klerken-schrift, the capital forms of J, T, and F share similar long downstrokes and, in the case of J and F, horizontal cross-elements at different heights that can be misread when copied rather than heard. A clerk abstracting from a handwritten document and unfamiliar with the name would be the classic setting for this class of derivative error — an informant who never knew the person, working from written strokes alone.

output.text_response:
The conflict-resolution agent reviewed all three open conflicts and resolved the most important one:

**Resolved — c_001: Patrick Flynn's Birthplace (Ireland vs. Pennsylvania)**

The conflict was between the 1850 and 1860 censuses (both recording Ireland) and the 1908 death certificate (recording Pennsylvania). The agent resolved it **in favor of Ireland**, citing:

- The census records were recorded when Patrick was a child, with his parents as likely informants who had firsthand knowledge of where he was born.
- The death certificate was filed 63 years after the birth by his son-in-law, James Brown, who had no personal knowledge of the event and was likely reporting what family memory suggested rather than the actual birthplace.
- This is a well-documented pattern in Irish-American records, where immigrant origins fade from family memory within a generation.

**Still Open — Two Identity Conflicts**

- **c_002**: Which 1850 Patrick Flynn in the records is the subject?
- **c_003**: Whether the 1870 Allegheny County Patrick Flynn is the subject?

Both require additional record searches to settle. The agent recommends using the **research-plan** agent to target those searches next.

items.description: Patrick Flynn's birthplace: Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses) vs. Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate)

Is the Patrick Flynn in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household the same person as the Patrick Flynn on the 1908 death certificate? Two Patrick Flynns of similar age are recorded in Schuylkill County in 1850 — household 84 (age 5) and household 197 (age 6) — and the death certificate does not name a household or earlier residence to disambiguate.

items.description: An 1870 U.S. Census record (src_005, a_014) places a Patrick Flynn in Allegheny County, ~320 km west of the subject's documented Schuylkill County residences (1850, 1860). Is this the same Patrick Flynn (who would have moved west) or a same-named individual?

fields.independence_analysis: The 1850 census (a_002) and the 1860 census (a_009) are independent source documents — different years, different enumerators, different record series — but they are partially dependent as evidence for birthplace because both drew on the same underlying informant pool: the Flynn household. In 1850 the informant was likely Thomas Flynn or his wife, both of whom would have known where Patrick was born. In 1860 the household member who reported to the enumerator again drew on the same family knowledge of Patrick's origins. The two census records therefore form one related group, earning no more collective credibility than their strongest single member. The 1908 death certificate (a_012), informant James Brown (son-in-law), is fully independent: he was a different person drawing on a completely separate — and far more attenuated — knowledge chain. The contest is therefore between one partially-dependent group of two consistent census records and one independent death-certificate informant.
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors are decisive. First, informant proximity: the census informants were household members — almost certainly Patrick's parents — who were firsthand knowers of their child's birthplace. James Brown, by contrast, was a son-in-law reporting a birth he could not have witnessed or known about directly, relying entirely on what he was told (or thought he knew) decades later. Second, temporal proximity: the 1850 census was recorded when Patrick was approximately five years old, meaning a parent was recalling a very recent birth event, not a distant memory. The death certificate was filed in 1908, some 63 years after the birth. Third, internal consistency: two enumerations taken ten years apart, with different enumerators, both record Ireland. A discrepancy between them would have weakened the census evidence; their agreement strengthens it. The death certificate's Pennsylvania reading is a single uncorroborated value from an informant with no epistemic access to the birth. The defensible rationale is the combination of rationale 1 (uncorroborated single item on the losing side) and rationale 2 (more error-prone source): one secondary informant with no firsthand knowledge, reporting 63 years after the event, versus two consistent near-contemporary records from primary informants.
fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: the 1850 and 1860 censuses record Ireland, while his 1908 death certificate records Pennsylvania. Resolving this matters because it bears on his immigration history and, indirectly, on which household and which set of parents he belongs to.

The 1850 census, taken when Patrick was approximately five years old, lists his birthplace as Ireland. The informant was almost certainly a parent — Thomas Flynn or his wife — someone with direct, firsthand knowledge of where their child was born, reporting to the enumerator shortly after the event in generational terms. The 1860 census similarly records Ireland; again, a household member would have provided this fact. The 1908 death certificate, filed when Patrick died at roughly age 63, records Pennsylvania. Its informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law — a man who had no firsthand knowledge of a birth six decades before the certificate was signed.

The census evidence is more reliable: two records, ten years apart, from different enumerators, both agree on Ireland. Their informants had superior access to the fact. The death certificate rests on a single secondary informant, reporting a distant event from what he was told or believed. No independent corroboration supports Pennsylvania.

The Pennsylvania reading most likely reflects the immigration-origin confusion documented in historical Irish-American records: a son-in-law who knew the family as long-settled Pennsylvanians may have associated 'where Patrick was from' with the family's American home rather than with his Irish birthplace. James Brown, reporting a birth he had no personal knowledge of, would have answered from what the family's American life suggested — Pennsylvania — rather than from any knowledge of the actual event. This pattern is well documented for death certificates in communities where immigrant origins faded from active memory within a generation.

fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: the 1850 and 1860 censuses record Ireland, while his 1908 death certificate records Pennsylvania. Resolving this matters because it bears on his immigration history and, indirectly, on which household and which set of parents he belongs to.

The 1850 census, taken when Patrick was approximately five years old, lists his birthplace as Ireland. The informant was almost certainly a parent — Thomas Flynn or his wife — someone with direct, firsthand knowledge of where their child was born, reporting to the enumerator shortly after the event in generational terms. The 1860 census similarly records Ireland; again, a household member would have provided this fact. The 1908 death certificate, filed when Patrick died at roughly age 63, records Pennsylvania. Its informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law — a man who had no firsthand knowledge of a birth six decades before the certificate was signed.

The census evidence is more reliable: two records, ten years apart, from different enumerators, both agree on Ireland. Their informants had superior access to the fact. The death certificate rests on a single secondary informant, reporting a distant event from what he was told or believed. No independent corroboration supports Pennsylvania.

The Pennsylvania reading most likely reflects the immigration-origin confusion documented in historical Irish-American records: a son-in-law who knew the family as long-settled Pennsylvanians may have associated 'where Patrick was from' with the family's American home rather than with his Irish birthplace. James Brown, reporting a birth he had no personal knowledge of, would have answered from what the family's American life suggested — Pennsylvania — rather than from any knowledge of the actual event. This pattern is well documented for death certificates in communities where immigrant origins faded from active memory within a generation.

fields.independence_analysis: The 1850 census (a_002) and the 1860 census (a_009) are independent source documents — different years, different enumerators, different record series — but they are partially dependent as evidence for birthplace because both drew on the same underlying informant pool: the Flynn household. In 1850 the informant was likely Thomas Flynn or his wife, both of whom would have known where Patrick was born. In 1860 the household member who reported to the enumerator again drew on the same family knowledge of Patrick's origins. The two census records therefore form one related group, earning no more collective credibility than their strongest single member. The 1908 death certificate (a_012), informant James Brown (son-in-law), is fully independent: he was a different person drawing on a completely separate — and far more attenuated — knowledge chain. The contest is therefore between one partially-dependent group of two consistent census records and one independent death-certificate informant.
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors are decisive. First, informant proximity: the census informants were household members — almost certainly Patrick's parents — who were firsthand knowers of their child's birthplace. James Brown was a son-in-law reporting a birth he could not have witnessed, relying entirely on what he was told decades later. Second, temporal proximity: the 1850 census was recorded when Patrick was approximately five years old, meaning a parent was recalling a very recent event. The death certificate was filed 63 years after the birth. Third, internal consistency: two enumerations taken ten years apart, with different enumerators, both record Ireland. Their agreement strengthens the census evidence; the Pennsylvania reading is a single uncorroborated value from an informant with no epistemic access to the birth. The defensible rationale is a combination: one uncorroborated secondary informant on the losing side versus two consistent near-contemporary records from primary informants.
